Every byte-priced table declares a unit; a test fails if one is missing

No test asserts a pricing constant without an accompanying provenance reference

context: Plan: /Users/joe/.claude/plans/stateful-purring-axolotl.md (PR A, Step 2). Reuse precedent, not invention: repo pattern is scripts/generate_<x>.py with a --check drift mode.
description:
The pricing table has no provenance model and its only automated safeguard is anchored to a date that cannot be true.

Provenance: add a per-table provenance block (source URL, retrieved date, upstream_published, method: api|manual|derived_from_announcement, verified_regions). Per table, not per leaf - a table comes from one API call. Model it on _project/joinorder/tiny_reference_cardinalities.json, which pairs file-level provenance with per-entry checksums. Do NOT try to reuse _project/scripts/audit_sha_check.py: it binds narrative claims to a BenchBox git SHA, not a value to a vendor URL.

Fix the false metadata (R16): metadata.last_updated '2025-11-09' is not a refresh date. git log --follow shows values were authored in e0438e993 (2026-02-04, initial release) and only relocated Python->YAML in 8281615b0 (2026-05-22); no value was ever changed. The claimed date also predates the repo's first commit. Replace with honest per-table values - method: manual, retrieved: unknown - wherever that is the truth.

Units: replace the single global BYTES_PER_TB = 1024**4 in calculator.py:35 with a per-table unit declaration carried through the lookup result and a BYTES_PER_UNIT map. BigQuery declares tebibyte (vendor-confirmed: its own worked example divides by 1099511627776). Athena and Synapse declare terabyte_unconfirmed, which resolves to 1024**4 so behavior is unchanged, and is the flag the follow-up contract work must resolve. Encoding the uncertainty in data is the point.

Tests: the current pricing tests assert the table against itself (assert price == 0.0833), so they cannot fail when a price is wrong and they force a lockstep edit when one is corrected. Replace with: (1) reachability - every workload_type/node type/edition production can emit resolves without fallback, which is the test that would have caught C1 at authoring time; (2) fail-closed - an unknown key yields no value and an unavailable end-to-end cost_status; (3) provenance completeness - every table has provenance, every byte-priced table declares a unit; (4) a small number of golden values, each annotated with the provenance key it came from so it reads as a citation rather than a magic number.
